nameStory: The Northern Crescent gets its name from the delicate crescent-shaped markings that decorate its wings like tiny moons. The 'northern' part distinguishes it from its close cousin, the Pearl Crescent, as this species prefers cooler climates and is found further north across New England.
description: The Northern Crescent is a small, orange and black butterfly that dances through New England's meadows and woodland edges during summer. With a wingspan of just over an inch (32-38 mm), it's about the size of a large coin. Its wings display intricate patterns of orange patches outlined in black, with distinctive crescent-shaped white spots that give the butterfly its name. This delicate member of the brush-footed butterfly family is a common sight from June through July.

idTips.label: Wing crescents
idTips.description: Look for small, white crescent-shaped spots along the wing edges - they're clearest on the hindwings and catch the light like tiny pearls

idTips.label: Orange and black pattern
idTips.description: Wings show bright orange patches outlined with black veining, creating a stained-glass window effect when sunlight shines through

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: About the size of a quarter when wings are spread, much smaller than monarchs or swallowtails you might see in the same areas

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a bouncy, erratic pattern close to the ground, often landing with wings spread flat on flowers or warm surfaces

idTips.label: Preferred flowers
idTips.description: Often seen nectaring on white clover, dogbane, and fleabane - will sit still long enough for close observation while feeding

habitat: Northern Crescents prefer sunny, open areas throughout New England including meadows, old fields, woodland clearings, and forest edges. They're often found in areas where asters and other wildflowers in the sunflower family grow, since these plants serve as food for their caterpillars. You'll spot them in both rural countryside and suburban areas with naturalized grasslands.

seasonality.spring: Not yet active - still in chrysalis form from the previous year's late-summer caterpillars.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through July when adults emerge, mate, and lay eggs. This is the best time to spot them nectaring on flowers during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Adults have finished their life cycle, but caterpillars may still be feeding on aster plants before forming chrysalises for winter.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as chrysalises attached to plant stems or hidden in leaf litter, completely dormant until spring warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: Northern Crescent caterpillars are picky eaters that will only munch on plants in the aster family - but when they become adults, they completely change their dining preferences and can only sip liquid nectar, having lost the ability to chew solid food entirely!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Pearl Crescent, which looks nearly identical. The Northern Crescent tends to be slightly larger and has more distinct white crescents on the wing undersides - think 'Northern = more noticeable crescents' as a memory trick.
compareHints: Compared to the Pearl Crescent, the Northern Crescent is generally larger and shows more prominent white crescents on the underwing surfaces. While Pearl Crescents can have multiple broods per year, Northern Crescents typically have just one generation annually. Both species can be found in similar habitats, but Northern Crescents are more common in cooler, northern areas of New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pearl Crescents are distinguished from Northern Crescents by their broader range throughout New England and the clearer, more contrasted pearl crescent mark on the hindwing underside.
